judge_assessment.explanation: The false claim is in answer_key.pdf problem 6 exactly as quoted: 'the least-squares line is fitted so that the residuals sum to zero. The positive and negative residuals must therefore balance, which puts roughly half the points above the line and half below. A line with, say, seven of eight points above it could not be the least-squares line.' Zero residual SUM constrains signed magnitudes, not counts — a fit with seven small positive residuals and one large negative residual sums to zero and is a perfectly ordinary least-squares line for right-skewed residuals, so the last sentence is flatly wrong and the 'must therefore' inference is invalid. The judge is also right that the defect is not confined to the key: worksheet.pdf problem 6 asks the student to 'Explain in one sentence why a least-squares line is expected to split the points roughly this way', which builds the false generalisation into the task itself, so a correct student who answers 'it does not have to' is marked wrong. And the artifact finding is precise: verify.json id 6 is {'type': 'probability', 'favorable': 4, 'total': 8, 'expected': '1/2'} — it checks the observed count in THIS data set and can say nothing about the general property the stem demands. Everything else the judge validated, I re-derived and confirm: the line really is the least-squares fit for the printed data (Sxy = 252, Sxx = 42, slope 6, intercept 79 - 6(4.5) = 52), r = 252/sqrt(42*1584) = 0.977, r^2 = 0.954529 -> 0.955, predictions 82 at x=5 and 100 at x=8, residual 85 - 82 = 3, mean score 632/8 = 79 which equals 52 + 6(4.5), unexplained variation 4.5%, and the extrapolation 52 + 6(20) = 172. The author half-saw the problem — the grading note says 'Exactly half is not guaranteed in general — roughly half is the claim' — and still printed the impossibility sentence, which makes this a hedge rather than a correction.

strengths_to_preserve: The data set is not decorative: x = 1..8 with y = 61, 61, 67, 79, 85, 85, 91, 103 really does have least-squares line yhat = 52 + 6x and r = 0.977, and every residual is exactly plus or minus 3. A student who recomputes anything on this sheet gets the printed numbers, and problem 7's point-of-averages check (52 + 6(4.5) = 79 = ybar) lands exactly because the data was constructed to make it land.

Problem 9 into problem 10(a) is the best-built pair in the packet: the student first computes 172 on a 120-point exam, then has to use that impossible number as the evidence for why extrapolation outside 1-8 hours is unsupported. The key's grading note requires precisely that ('part (a) needs the observed range 1 to 8 hours named and the impossible value used as evidence').

Problem 10(b)'s manual rubric goes past 'correlation is not causation': it requires a named confounder, requires a randomised design, explains why random assignment is what removes the confounder, and explicitly rejects the common non-answer — 'a larger sample or a stronger correlation is not a fix ... more data from an observational study cannot remove a confounder'.

The two declared traps are the right two for this topic and both print in the key's Common wrong answers block with their values: -3 on problem 3 (predicted minus observed, which reverses every interpretation) and 95.5 on problem 8 (explained instead of unexplained variation).

The scatter plot renders the fitted line together with the eight points at readable scale (pgfplots, width 11cm, gridded, axis limits 0-9 by 50-112), so problem 6's counting task is genuinely answerable from the display rather than requiring the student to imagine the line.

root_causes.description: A general mathematical property was invented rather than recalled, and it was written into both the worksheet stem and the answer key. The true property — the least-squares line passes through (xbar, ybar) and its residuals sum to zero — was already used correctly in problem 7; problem 6 then over-extends it from magnitudes to counts and asserts an impossibility ('seven of eight points above ... could not be the least-squares line') that is simply untrue. Because the sheet's own data splits 4-4, the false rule was never contradicted by the case at hand.
evidence: answer_key.pdf problem 6: 'The positive and negative residuals must therefore balance, which puts roughly half the points above the line and half below. A line with, say, seven of eight points above it could not be the least-squares line.'
worksheet.pdf problem 6: 'Explain in one sentence why a least-squares line is expected to split the points roughly this way.'
answer_key.pdf problem 6 grading note: 'Exactly half is not guaranteed in general — roughly half is the claim' — the hedge acknowledges the risk without withdrawing the impossibility claim.
Counterexample the sheet never tests: residuals +1, +1, +1, +1, +1, +1, +1, -7 sum to zero, so seven of eight points lie above a legitimate least-squares fit.

root_causes.description: Five printed slots ask for written statements and only one is declared manual, so the pipeline had no place to record that problem 6's required explanation is the risky part of the item. verify.json id 6 verifies the observed fraction 4/8 = 1/2, which is true and irrelevant to the claim the student must produce, and the gate reports green.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 3 ('say in one sentence whether the line under-predicted or over-predicted'), 5 ('Compare your prediction with the observed score'), 6 ('Explain in one sentence why...'), 7 ('What property of the least-squares line does this confirm?') and 9 ('state what is wrong with the number you get') all print explanation slots.
verify.json declares exactly one manual entry, id 10.
verify.json id 6: {'type': 'probability', 'favorable': 4, 'total': 8, 'expected': '1/2'} — the count in this data set, not the general property.
gate_log.txt reports the chain passing; the judge's own artifact finding says machine verification 'checks the observed fraction but does not test the false explanatory generalization'.

improvements.title: Require a general property asserted in a stem or key to be stated as the theorem actually guarantees
improvements.proposed_change: Add a rule and a checklist entry: whenever a stem or key states a property of a method ('a least-squares line is expected to...', 'this must always...', 'could not be...'), the author must (a) name the theorem being invoked and (b) state the property in the theorem's own terms. Sum-of-residuals-is-zero licenses statements about signed magnitudes and about the line passing through the point of averages; it licenses nothing about counts of points on each side. Add a short entry to references/problem-library.md for the regression strand listing the properties that ARE guaranteed (passes through (xbar, ybar); residuals sum to zero; r^2 is the explained share of variance) alongside the three attractive falsehoods (equal counts above and below; r^2 measures linearity of the true relationship; a high r licenses extrapolation), so this topic is authored from a checked list rather than from recall. For this case, problem 6 should ask for the property that IS true — that the residuals sum to zero, verifiable from the printed +3/-3 pattern — and the key's impossibility sentence must be deleted.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture answer-key source containing 'seven of eight points above it could not be the least-squares line' with a verify.json whose only regression entry is the observed 4/8 fraction. The claim lint must exit non-zero, naming the unsupported generalisation and the fact that no entry establishes it. Rewriting the sentence to the residual-sum statement, or declaring a property entry that the checker can test, makes it pass.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes this case's hard failure and the class it belongs to — correct arithmetic wrapped around an invented theorem, which currently survives every gate because the sheet's own numbers happen to be consistent with it. This is the one defect here that would actively teach a student something false.
improvements.risk: A lint over property language will fire on legitimate teaching sentences ('the median is resistant', 'the mean is a balance point'), so it must be a review checkpoint for the regression/statistics strands with an author acknowledgement, not a blunt keyword block, or authors will strip useful explanation to get past it.

improvements.title: Declare problems 3, 5, 6, 7 and 9's written statements as manual items instead of only problem 10
improvements.proposed_change: Require a manual entry for every stem containing an explanation or statement verb, with a desc that records what the grader must accept. Applied here, problem 6's manual entry would have forced the author to write down the acceptance criterion for 'why a least-squares line splits the points roughly this way' — the step at which the invented rule would have had to be justified. Generate the manual count in final_response.md from verify.json so the reported figure (one) cannot understate five open slots.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture with curr-448's worksheet source and verify.json: the gate must exit non-zero listing problems 3, 5, 6, 7 and 9 as explanation slots with no manual entry, while problem 10 passes. Adding manual entries with descs makes the fixture pass and makes the generated manual count read six.
improvements.expected_impact: Correct grading accounting, and — more importantly here — a forcing function that puts every asserted explanation in front of the author as a declared, written acceptance criterion instead of leaving it inside key prose that nothing inspects.
improvements.risk: Short interpretive riders attached to verified numbers ('say whether it under-predicted') are much cheaper to grade than problem 10's paragraph; listing them identically will overstate the grading burden unless the manual list distinguishes brief riders from full open synthesis.

case_summary: A carefully constructed regression sheet — the eight-point data set genuinely yields yhat = 52 + 6x with r = 0.977, all residuals are exactly +/-3, and the point-of-averages check in problem 7 lands exactly — that fails on one invented theorem. Problem 6's stem asks the student to explain why a least-squares line 'is expected to split the points roughly this way', and the key backs it with the claim that residuals summing to zero forces roughly equal counts above and below, adding that seven of eight points above 'could not be the least-squares line'. Zero sum balances signed magnitudes, not counts, so the sentence is false and the required student explanation is false with it; residuals +1 seven times and -7 once sum to zero. The REJECT is right. Machine verification could not help: verify.json id 6 checks the observed 4/8 fraction, which is true and beside the point, and only problem 10 of five explanation slots is declared manual, so no acceptance criterion for problem 6's reasoning was ever written down. The extrapolation pair (9 into 10a) and problem 10(b)'s confounder-and-design rubric are the strongest parts of the packet and should survive any revision.
